title: Why does losing hurt more?
principle: A loss hurts about twice as much as an equal gain pleases.

screens.text: Let me offer you a bet. I toss a coin. Tails, you pay me ₹100. Heads, I pay you ₹150. You can win more than you can lose. Will you play? Most people say no. Nobel Prize winner Daniel Kahneman wrote about bets like this.

screens.title: Why say no?
screens.text: Play this bet many times, and you win more than you lose. Half the time you win ₹150, half the time you lose ₹100. But most people fear losing ₹100 more than they want to win ₹150.

screens.prompt: In 1992, Tversky and Kahneman studied how much worse a loss feels than an equal gain. What did they find?
screens.why: In their study, a loss felt about 2.25 times as bad as an equal gain felt good. Other studies find different numbers, some lower, some higher. But "about twice" is a useful rule.

screens.title: Loss aversion
screens.text: This is called loss aversion. Losing money hurts about twice as much as winning the same amount feels good. Losing ₹100 can feel as bad as winning ₹200 feels good. This also helps explain why a price rise hurts more than an equal price cut feels good.

screens.title: It's used on you
screens.text: Shops use this on you every day. "Free delivery above ₹499" makes you add a snack to avoid paying ₹40 for delivery. "Your cart will expire soon!" makes you fear losing your items. You often spend more to avoid a small loss.

screens.prompt: Let's do a sum. Cart: ₹450. Delivery: ₹40, free above ₹499. You add a ₹60 snack you didn't need. How much more did you pay?
screens.why: Right. Without the snack: ₹450 + ₹40 = ₹490. With it: ₹510. You paid ₹20 more for a snack you didn't need, just to avoid paying ₹40 for delivery.

wrong.a: Delivery became free, but you paid ₹60 for the snack. Without it: ₹450 + ₹40 = ₹490. With it: ₹510. That's ₹20 more.
wrong.c: The snack cost ₹60, but you saved ₹40 on delivery. Without it: ₹490. With it: ₹510. You paid ₹20 more.

screens.title: Now look at your business
screens.text: Your buyers feel the same fear. It's June. You start baking for a new colony across town. Families there don't know you. Paying ₹850 for a cake from someone new feels risky: they could lose ₹850.

screens.prompt: Quick sum. A family may lose ₹850 on a new baker. A loss feels about twice as big. How good must it feel, in rupees?
screens.why: Yes. ₹850 × 2 = about ₹1,700. One cake can't promise that much. So promising a bigger gain won't work.

wrong.a: That makes the risk half as big. A loss feels about twice as bad, so the win must feel like ₹850 × 2 = about ₹1,700.
wrong.b: That means a loss and a win feel equal. A loss feels about twice as bad: ₹850 × 2 = about ₹1,700.

screens.setup: It's June. In the new colony, 30 families saw your post, but only 2 ordered. Your cake sells for ₹850. It costs ₹400 to make, so you keep ₹450. You can bake 20 cakes a week.
screens.question: How do you get families to try you?

options.label: "Only 5 cakes left this week!"
options.outcome: 3 families order quickly. The next week, you post "Only 5 cakes left!" again. A family sees the same message twice. She tells the colony group, and orders stop.
options.why: You can bake 20 cakes a week, so "only 5 left" was not true. Fake limits may work once, but then buyers who hear about it stop trusting you.
options.better: "Not happy? Full money back." Remove their risk.

options.label: "Not happy? Full money back, no questions."
options.outcome: 12 families order. One asks for her money back, and you pay her ₹850 at once. You still earn ₹4,550: 11 cakes at ₹450, minus ₹400 for the refunded cake. Next month, 8 order again.
options.why: You removed their risk. If the cake was bad, they could get their money back. So they no longer feared losing ₹850.

options.label: ₹200 off the first cake
options.outcome: 6 families order at ₹650. Each cake leaves you ₹250: ₹1,500 in all. Some ask, "Why so cheap? Is it old?" Next month, 2 come back at ₹850.
options.why: A small saving doesn't remove the fear of losing ₹650 on a bad cake. And a discount can make a good cake seem poor.
options.better: "Not happy? Full money back." Remove their risk.

screens.title: Remove the risk
screens.text: Here's the fair way to use this. A money-back offer takes the risk off the buyer, so trying your cake feels safe. If buyers can't lose money, they don't need to feel they're getting ₹1,700 worth to say yes.

screens.title: The honest line
screens.text: Remember the line: use on others only what you'd accept being used on you. Removing a buyer's risk is fair. Fake deadlines and repeated "you'll lose!" messages scare buyers. Use loss aversion to remove a buyer's fear, never to create it.
A ___ hurts about twice as much as an equal ___ pleases.
screens.why: Exactly. That's why most people refuse the coin toss. And why "money back" helps new families decide to buy.

summary: Loss aversion: losing money hurts about twice as much as winning the same amount feels good.
"Free delivery above ₹499" and "your cart will expire" use this fear. Do the sum before you add another item.
Use it fairly: remove the buyer's risk, so trying feels safe. No fake deadlines.

cards.back: ₹510 instead of ₹490. Trying to avoid a small "loss" can make you spend more.
